questions.stem: Scenario S2. A team places a CLAUDE.md in the folder of its payments service and expects every session in the repository to carry its rules from the first message. Sessions that never touch that folder do not show them. What explains it?

options.text: The file loads only for sessions started by its owner, since it is a personal setting
options.says: Ruled out because the scope table gives a directory file to "Whoever works in that subdirectory", and not to its author alone.

options.text: The file loads at launch but is pushed out first when context fills, since it has the lowest rank
options.says: Ruled out because the page names launch loading for "The root `CLAUDE.md` and the rule files without a `paths` list".

options.text: The file loads on demand, since files in subdirectories load only when read
options.says: A CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory is not loaded at launch but when Claude reads files in that directory (module 71, page 1). The page's words are "Files in subdirectories load on demand when Claude reads files in those directories."

options.text: The file loads only when a slash command names it, since commands choose memory
options.says: Ruled out because the page says a subdirectory file "is not loaded at launch", and nothing in it ties its loading to a command.

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A repository holds a command file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and, after a refactor, also a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md. A developer types /deploy. What runs?

options.text: Both, one after the other, since the name maps to each file
options.says: Ruled out because one name leads to one definition: "A skill beats a command file of the same name."

options.text: The packaged definition, since it wins on a shared name
options.says: Custom commands have been merged into skills, and when a skill and a command file share a name the skill wins (module 71, page 1). Existing command files keep working. The page puts it as "when a skill and a command file share a name the skill wins".

options.text: Neither, since a clash of names disables the command
options.says: Ruled out because "the existing command files keep working", and the name resolves to the skill.

options.text: The command file, since older definitions keep their place
options.says: Ruled out because an older file gets no priority on a clash, and the skill wins: "when a skill and a command file share a name the skill wins"; the older files keep working only where no skill shares the name.

origin.section: The audit: a checklist that reads the files

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A rule file in a project's rules folder has no paths list. The team assumes that it applies only to the files its title mentions. When does it load?

options.text: At the start of every session, since nothing restricts its scope
options.says: The root file and the rule files without a paths list load at the start of every session at the same priority, so a rule meant for one area then costs context everywhere (module 71, page 1). The page puts it as "The root CLAUDE.md and the rule files without a paths list load at the start of every session, at the same priority".

options.text: Never, since an unscoped rule has no target
options.says: Ruled out because the audit's finding `rule-loads-always` reports "a rule with no `paths` list".

options.text: Only when a developer names it in a command, since unscoped rules wait for a call
options.says: Ruled out because "Without frontmatter it behaves like part of the project file and loads at launch.", so no command is needed.

options.text: Only when a file of its area is opened, since rules load by relevance
options.says: Ruled out because the page says a rule with a `paths` list loads "when Claude works with a file that matches one of its globs", and this one has none.

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A rule file for handlers lists the path pattern src/api/*.ts, and a developer opens src/api/v2/orders.ts. Does the rule load?

options.text: No, since rule files read only exact file names
options.says: Ruled out because a `paths` entry is "A `paths` entry is a glob", and globs match by pattern.

options.text: Yes, since the extension alone decides the match
options.says: Ruled out because the page's example is "`src/api/**/*.ts` reaches every TypeScript file below `src/api/`", which needs the double star.

options.text: Yes, since a star matches any depth below the folder
options.says: Ruled out because a single star does not cross folders: "`**` crosses folders and `*` stays inside one", and the documentation's table shows "`src/**/*` for all files under `src/`".

options.text: No, since a lone star stays within one level
options.says: In a paths glob the double star crosses folders and the single star stays inside one, so src/api/*.ts misses a file one level deeper (module 71, page 1). The page's example is src/api/**/*.ts for every TypeScript file below src/api/. The page puts it as "** crosses folders and * stays inside one".

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A repository keeps shared guidance in AGENTS.md beside its memory file, and a developer adds a CLAUDE.local.md for their notes. Afterwards the assistant stops following the shared guidance. What explains it?

options.text: The personal file overrides the shared guidance line by line
options.says: Ruled out because "All discovered files are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other".

options.text: Local files switch off every shared file in the repository
options.says: Ruled out because only AGENTS.md is skipped, because "the local file counts as a CLAUDE.md".

options.text: Only one family is read, so its sibling needs importing
options.says: The local file counts as a CLAUDE.md, so Claude reads only CLAUDE.md files and AGENTS.md is skipped unless it is imported or the setting is changed (module 57, page 1). The page puts it as "reads only your CLAUDE.md files".

options.text: AGENTS.md is read only in unattended runs
options.says: Ruled out because the file "is skipped unless you import it or change the setting", whatever the kind of run.

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A team asks for a validation function with a paragraph of description, and the output handles the main scenario but guesses at awkward values. What does the page add to the prompt?

options.text: Two or three worked pairs with expected answers, one at a boundary
options.says: Examples of input and output give the work a target: two or three cases with their expected results say what a paragraph of description leaves open, and the page's example is one valid address, one invalid and one edge (module 71, page 2). The page puts it as "Two or three cases with their expected results say what a paragraph of description leaves open".

options.text: A request to plan before coding, with no worked pairs shown beside it
options.says: Ruled out because a plan changes the order and not the target: "Plan mode tells Claude to research and propose changes without making them", while "Claude stops when the work looks done".

options.text: A longer paragraph on how careful and exact the code must be
options.says: Ruled out because a paragraph is what leaves the cases open: "say what a paragraph of description leaves open".

options.text: A larger model, to infer the awkward inputs
options.says: Ruled out because the first recommendation is "Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare."

questions.stem: Scenario S2. To avoid match failures, a developer tells Claude Code to rewrite the whole document for a one-line fix in an existing source file. What does the page say?

options.text: Keep the whole-file write if the file is under a hundred lines
options.says: Ruled out because the page gives no size exception: "For partial changes to an existing file, use Edit."

options.text: Use the edit tool, since replacing everything lets damage slip through unseen
options.says: Write overwrites with the full content, so an accidental change elsewhere goes unseen, and for partial changes to an existing file the page says to use Edit (module 56, page 1). The page puts it as "Write overwrites with the full content, so an accidental change elsewhere goes unseen".

options.text: Use the search tool, since it can find the line and also replace it
options.says: Ruled out because the search tool only reads: the table gives `Grep` the job "Searches file contents", and the replacing job to Edit: "Replaces one exact string with another in a file".

options.text: Keep the whole-file write, since it never fails to match
options.says: Ruled out because the page names the cost of a whole-file write: "A wrong tool choice costs tokens and, with Write, risks the rest of the file."

questions.stem: Scenario S2. A team writes one skill for each kind of code, expecting each skill to apply by itself whenever a file of its kind is opened. What happens?

options.text: Each skill applies when its folder is opened, since folders are the unit of loading
options.says: Ruled out because the page's rule files, not skills, carry "a `paths` list of globs".

options.text: Each skill applies by itself, since skills watch the open files
options.says: Ruled out because "Skills load when they are invoked or chosen, not because a path matched."

options.text: Only the newest skill applies, since later skills outrank earlier ones
options.says: Ruled out because skills do not replace each other by age: "A project-root skill and a nested one with one name both load".

options.text: Matching a path never launches one, since scoped rules are what load by location
options.says: A skill is invoked, or chosen by the model from its description, and a path match does not start it, so conventions that must apply by path go in rule files with a paths list (module 71, page 1). The page puts it as "a skill is invoked, or chosen by the model from its description, and a path match does not start it".

questions.stem: Scenario S3. Before synthesis even starts, the lead of a four-worker research team has no room left because every worker returned everything it fetched. Which change fits?

options.text: The coordinator condenses each output in its own context and keeps the summary
options.says: Ruled out because the failure shows as "The coordinator's context fills with the raw output of its subagents", and condensing starts only after that output has arrived.

options.text: The synthesis agent receives every output directly, without the coordinator
options.says: Ruled out because "The coordinator is the only place where the pieces meet."

options.text: Each worker returns its full output split over several shorter messages
options.says: Ruled out because "only its final message returns to the parent", so the output arrives in one message, whatever its size.

options.text: Each one saves its results outside and hands back a lightweight reference
options.says: Large results should not travel through the hub: subagents store their work in external systems and pass lightweight references back (module 72, page 1). The page's table names the failure "Large results passed through the hub".

origin.section: Read a symptom as a failure shape

questions.stem: Scenario S3. The search agent is given a tool that writes notes to a shared drive so that findings are saved, and the report agent is given web search to check a figure. A review applies the least-privilege rule. What does it conclude?

options.text: Trim each to its own job, since each holds the other's kind of access
options.says: The search agent has the web tools and nothing that writes, and the report agent writes the report and calls nothing else, so each tool set is trimmed to the job (module 72, page 1). The least-privilege rule applies to each of the four subagents. The page puts it as "The search agent has the web tools and nothing that writes".

options.text: Both are right, since extra tools make the agents more flexible
options.says: Ruled out because "more tools make each choice less reliable".

options.text: Only the report agent is wrong, since the search agent must be able to save its findings
options.says: Ruled out because "an agent outside its specialisation misuses what it holds", and a note-writing tool is outside the search agent's job.

options.text: Both are right if each tool is logged, since logging controls the risk
options.says: Ruled out because the least-privilege rule of module 54 "applies to each of the four", and a log acts after the privilege exists.

questions.stem: Scenario S3. A search for one scope fails at first, and a retry through an alternative query later succeeds. The report's list of errors still shows the first failure. What is wrong?

options.text: The scope should be marked partial, since an error once occurred there
options.says: Ruled out because the status is "complete when every required scope has an `ok` result with at least one finding", and the retry gave this scope one.

options.text: The retry should have been hidden from the coordinator
options.says: Ruled out because the coordinator "decides" among alternatives, and it can decide "only if the error says what failed and what could be tried".

options.text: It should have been removed, since a newer result covered that topic
options.says: An error that a later result for the same scope made up for is dropped from the list of errors, since the report should list what is still wrong (module 72, page 2). The page puts it as "the report should list what is still wrong".

options.text: Nothing, since the list is a history of every failure that occurred
options.says: Ruled out because "an error that a later result for the same scope made up for is dropped from the list of errors".

origin.section: Partial is information and it is not coverage

questions.stem: Scenario S3. A tool in a subagent's chain keeps failing, and the subagent simply stops with a generic message. The team wants the system to adapt. Which behaviour does Anthropic's article support?

options.text: End the whole run at the first failure so that nothing wrong is reported
options.says: Ruled out because "Send the timeout to a top-level handler that ends the whole run" is rejected, because "the scopes that worked are lost with it".

options.text: Tell the worker about the broken step, so that it adjusts
options.says: The article says "Letting the agent know when a tool is failing and letting it adapt works surprisingly well", which is why a failure comes back as a result with its type, its query and alternatives (module 72, page 1).

options.text: Return an empty result marked successful so that the run continues
options.says: Ruled out because "it turns a failure into a false answer, and nothing downstream can recover from a failure it was never told about".

options.text: Hide the failure from the agent so that it keeps its plan
options.says: Ruled out because a plan cannot change on an error it never saw: the coordinator "can decide only if the error says what failed and what could be tried".

origin.section: Read a symptom as a failure shape

questions.stem: Scenario S3. A search subagent hits a rate limit twice and succeeds on the third try, and the team's design passes every failure up to the coordinator for a decision. What does the page recommend?

options.text: Keep passing everything up to the coordinator, which sees the whole run
options.says: Ruled out because "Pass every failure up; the coordinator decides about retries" is rejected.

options.text: Report "search unavailable" and keep the report short
options.says: Ruled out because the coordinator cannot choose a recovery without "the failure type, the query, the partial results and the alternatives".

options.text: Stop the run and tell the user that it failed outright
options.says: Ruled out because "terminating on a single failure throws away the work of the other subagents".

options.text: Handle passing faults locally, and send up only what stays unresolved
options.says: Transient failures are handled locally, and only what the subagent cannot resolve goes up, with what was attempted and the partial results (module 66, page 1). The page says "transient failures are handled locally".

questions.stem: Scenario S3. To spare the coordinator's context, a developer lets the search and analysis subagents pass findings directly to each other. What does the page say?

options.text: Allow it, since a shorter path saves tokens for the coordinator's own window
options.says: Ruled out because "Let the subagents pass findings to each other to save the coordinator's context" is rejected.

options.text: Allow only a route through the hub, since that gives one place to observe
options.says: All communication runs through the coordinator, for observability, one way of handling errors and control over what flows where (module 46, page 1). The page's words are "all communication runs through the coordinator".

options.text: Allow it if each pair logs its exchanges to a shared file
options.says: Ruled out because "A subagent does not know the user's original question, the plan, the other subagents", so no pair has an exchange to log.

options.text: Allow it for the analysis agent only, since it reads documents
options.says: Ruled out because "The coordinator is the only place where the pieces meet."

questions.stem: Scenario S3. To keep the writer's input short, the coordinator has the synthesis step compress all findings into prose and tells the writer to add sources afterwards. What does the page say?

options.text: It is sound for numbers only, since prose carries words well but not figures
options.says: Ruled out because the loss is not limited to figures: "It is lost the moment a step turns findings into prose".

options.text: It is sound, since short input is easier for the writer to draft
options.says: Ruled out because "Summarise the findings first; the writer will add sources later" is rejected.

options.text: It is unsound, since claim-origin pairs must travel and sentences cannot restore them
options.says: The sources are lost in the compression and cannot be rebuilt from prose, so the claim-source mappings travel through every step (module 69, page 1). The page puts it as "the claim-source mappings travel through every step".

options.text: It is sound if the writer searches again for each claim it makes
options.says: Ruled out because "the sources are lost in the compression and cannot be rebuilt from prose".

questions.stem: Scenario S3. A report's table gives a figure with no mention of the survey behind it, and a reader later sees it disagree with an audit figure and takes it for an error. What was left out?

options.text: The method, since it is part of the finding
options.says: The method is part of the finding, and without it a disagreement between a survey and an audit looks like an error (module 69, page 2). The page puts it as "the method is part of the finding".

options.text: The reader's rank, since figures vary by audience
options.says: Ruled out because the omission is a field of the finding and not a fact of the audience: "These are fields of the finding like the source and the date".

options.text: A rounding note, since small differences come from rounding
options.says: Ruled out because "A figure from a survey and a figure from an audit are not interchangeable", which is a difference of method and not of rounding.

options.text: A longer sentence, since tables lack context by nature
options.says: Ruled out because the table is not the fault: "Financial and other numeric data: a table."

questions.stem: Scenario S4. To make a ticket tool safer, a developer writes a settings rule that denies it only when the argument names a closed ticket, using a parenthesised pattern on the MCP tool. What does the rule do?

options.text: It denies the whole server, since parentheses widen the pattern
options.says: Ruled out because the whole-server form carries no parentheses: "A rule can name a whole server".

options.text: It narrows the tool to closed tickets, as path patterns narrow file tools
options.says: Ruled out because the page narrows a server by name: "allow the reading tools by name and deny the others by name".

options.text: It asks the user for each ticket, since a pattern implies a prompt
options.says: Ruled out because "In a settings file, a deny rule with parentheses on an MCP tool is skipped", so it never reaches the point of asking.

options.text: It matches nothing, since an entry of that form is skipped
options.says: In a settings file a rule for an MCP tool that carries parentheses is skipped and matches nothing, so an argument pattern is not a way to narrow an MCP tool there (module 73, page 1). Allow or deny the tools by name. The page puts it as "In a settings file, a rule for an MCP tool that carries parentheses is skipped, so it matches nothing".

origin.section: MCP servers: one name in three places

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A team commits a .mcp.json whose ticket server's location is written with a fallback, and whose token is written with no fallback. A reviewer objects to the first. What is the verdict?

options.text: Wrong, since a non-secret entry is suited to a placeholder
options.says: The expression with a fallback expands to the variable if it is set and to the default otherwise, and a default is right for a value that is not secret and wrong for a token (module 73, page 1). The page puts it as "A default is right for a value that is not secret, such as the ticket server's address, and wrong for a token".

options.text: Wrong, since expansion does not work in the url field
options.says: Ruled out because expansion "works in a server's `command`, `args`, `env`, `url` and `headers`".

options.text: Right, but the token should have a default as well, for a working clone
options.says: Ruled out because "a default for a token would be a credential in the file".

options.text: Wrong, since a fallback in any field is a credential in the file
options.says: Ruled out because the address is meant to have one: "The ticket address has a default and is optional."

questions.stem: Scenario S4. An engineer investigated a payments module on Monday. Overnight a colleague rewrote half of it, and on Tuesday the engineer wants to carry on. Which session choice does the page key?

options.text: Run two fresh sessions and repeat the whole analysis in each, then merge the two
options.says: Ruled out because the choice is about "what the old context is worth", and repeating everything wastes the findings that still hold.

options.text: Begin anew with a short summary, since old results describe files as they were
options.says: Tool results in an old session describe files as they were, so after an overnight refactor the page keys a new session with a short structured summary and a fresh read of the files that matter (module 73, page 2). The page puts it as "Tool results in an old session describe files as they were".

options.text: Resume Monday's session, since the model remembers the analysis
options.says: Ruled out because "Resuming gives confident answers about code that is gone."

options.text: Fork Monday's session, since a branch keeps the analysis and the history
options.says: Ruled out because a fork is for "several directions" that start "from one shared analysis", not for code that changed.

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A pull request changes .mcp.json to add a new server, and the reviewer treats it as a configuration tweak. What does the page say?

options.text: It is reviewed by the platform team alone, since developers cannot judge servers
options.says: Ruled out because the sentence says "a pull request that changes `.mcp.json` deserves the review of a change to code".

options.text: It needs no review, since a configuration file cannot run code
options.says: Ruled out because "a server is code with access to your systems and a way into the model's context".

options.text: It needs scrutiny like code, since entries load unprompted in unattended runs
options.says: The project's servers load without a prompt in claude -p and SDK runs, so a pull request that changes .mcp.json deserves the review of a change to code (module 73, page 1). The page puts it as "The project's servers load without a prompt in claude -p and SDK runs".

options.text: It needs a review only if the server is remote, since local ones are trusted
options.says: Ruled out because the page trusts no origin by default: "A server that came with a repository is code from somebody else."

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A team denies the shell tool for its generator agent and concludes that the agent can no longer change files outside its folder. Is the conclusion sound?

options.text: Yes, since a deny rule on one tool covers its neighbours
options.says: Ruled out because "For files, an `Edit` rule applies to every built-in tool that edits files".

options.text: Yes, since all writes pass through the shell
options.says: Ruled out because "file permissions are checked against Edit and Read path rules only", and not against the shell.

options.text: No, but only because the agent could ask a person to approve
options.says: Ruled out because the rules are checked in the order "deny, then ask, then allow", and the file tools hold rules of their own.

options.text: No, since writing to disk has separate rules that must be set too
options.says: Denying the shell does not limit the file tools, which have their own rules, so the generator's writes must be limited by an Edit rule for its folder (module 73, page 1). The page puts it as "Denying the shell does not limit the file tools, which have their own rules".

origin.section: Writing in one folder: the rule must be about Edit

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A developer defines a server named github in their local scope with one address, and the committed file defines the same name with headers and another address. What does Claude Code use?

options.text: Only the highest-ranking entry, taken whole, since no merging happens there
options.says: The same name is connected once, using the entire entry from the highest-precedence source, so "The entire server entry from that source is used" (module 55, page 1).

options.text: A blend, headers from one and address from the other, since merging is the default
options.says: Ruled out because "fields are not merged across scopes".

options.text: The committed file's entry, since a team file always outranks a personal one
options.says: Ruled out because the order is "local, project, user, plugin-provided servers, then claude.ai connectors", so the local definition ranks above the committed one.

options.text: Both entries, connected twice, since each source keeps its own server
options.says: Ruled out because "Claude Code connects to it once, using the definition from the highest-precedence source".

origin.section: Three scopes: who loads it and who shares it

questions.stem: Scenario S4. Every integration in a team's setup is flagged to be present from the opening message of each session, on the theory that tools should always be at hand. What follows?

options.text: Costs fall, since the definitions are cached once they have been loaded
options.says: Ruled out because "each upfront tool consumes context that would otherwise be available for your conversation".

options.text: Crowded context and worse selection return, since lazy loading is bypassed
options.says: Loading every definition at the start brings back what tool search was avoiding: crowded context and worse selection (module 55, page 2). The page puts it as "Loading all of them at the start brings back what tool search was avoiding".

options.text: Selection improves, since the model sees every definition up front
options.says: Ruled out because "Tool selection accuracy degrades with more than 30-50 tools loaded at once".

options.text: Nothing, since definitions never count against the window
options.says: Ruled out because "the list costs context on every turn, since the definitions are sent each time".

questions.stem: Scenario S4. A team wants an exploring helper that cannot change anything and can also query the company's knowledge server, and an engineer says the built-in read-only explorer already does that. What is missing?

options.text: Nothing: the built-in one reaches every connected server
options.says: Ruled out because the built-in helper is "a read-only agent for file discovery, code search and codebase exploration", with no word of the team's own servers.

options.text: A longer root memory file that names the server
options.says: Ruled out because "the root file loads in every session and costs context each time".

options.text: A custom project agent whose tools include the lookup
options.says: Claude Code ships a read-only explorer itself, and a project subagent of your own can have the same read-only shape and be given the project's documentation server as well, with a tools line that lists only reading and searching tools (module 73, page 1). The page puts it as "a project subagent of your own can have the same read-only shape and be given the project's documentation server as well".

options.text: A prompt line telling the main agent to avoid writing
options.says: Ruled out because "A sentence in the prompt is a request that the model weighs; the `tools` line is a list the subagent cannot go beyond."

origin.section: Tools are a list, and leaving it out is the widest list

questions.stem: Scenario S5. A headless step fails with a model error, and the job is configured to re-run itself until it passes. What does the page advise?

options.text: Extend the job timeout, since a longer wait is more likely to bring success
options.says: Ruled out because "A longer job timeout only lets a loop run longer."

options.text: Turn the job green with an empty result, so that the pipeline moves forward
options.says: Ruled out because "A green job that said nothing is the failure the gate prevents".

options.text: Report the breakdown and let a person decide, since repeats add expense
options.says: When a run fails, re-running it repeats the cost with no reason to expect a different result, so the job reports the failure and a person decides (module 74, page 1). The page puts it as "When a run fails, re-running it repeats the cost with no reason to expect a different result".

options.text: Re-run until it passes, since transient faults clear on their own over time
options.says: Ruled out because a headless run needs an end and not an open-ended repeat: "A run with no person must end by itself", and a repeat brings "no reason to expect a different result".

questions.stem: Scenario S5. A review prompt defines severity levels in words only, and the team finds that mediums and lows are mixed up. What does the page add to the criteria?

options.text: A longer definition for each rating, since more words fix the boundary
options.says: Ruled out because longer wording changes nothing: "What changes it is naming the cases."

options.text: A request for fewer comments overall, since fewer means less noise in the output
options.says: Ruled out because "A sentence that asks for more care is a request; the criteria are the case list."

options.text: An instruction to be conservative and report only important issues
options.says: Ruled out because the vague phrases "do not say what to leave out", so they change nothing.

options.text: A worked example per rating, since it shows where the boundary lies
options.says: Criteria have three lists, and each severity carries one example, because the example shows the model where the line between medium and low is, which a definition alone does not (module 74, page 2). The page puts it as "the example shows the model where the line between medium and low is, which a definition alone does not".

questions.stem: Scenario S5. The pipeline's review step continues the very session that wrote the change, so that the context is already loaded. A reviewer asks why that is a finding. What is the reason?

options.text: It favours the author's work, since a clean slate is the sharper check
options.says: A reviewer should not be the author: a fresh context improves code review since Claude will not be biased toward code it just wrote, so the review runs as its own session (module 74, page 2). The page puts it as "A fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote".

options.text: It cannot run in a pipeline, since sessions are interactive by design
options.says: Ruled out because the page asks that "In a pipeline that means the review runs as its own session", and does not say that sessions are interactive only; the pipeline description sets "`session` is `fresh`".

options.text: It loses the findings of earlier runs, since they are discarded
options.says: Ruled out because the earlier findings are a separate need that the run is given on top of a fresh session: "The second thing a review needs is memory of its own earlier output" and "`context` includes `prior_findings`".

options.text: It costs more tokens, since the whole history is billed again
options.says: Ruled out because the page gives authorship and not billing as the problem: "A reviewer should not be the author."

origin.section: What the run knows: context, independence and the practice

questions.stem: Scenario S5. A team runs a large review three times and keeps only the issues that two of the three runs report. Why does the page reject this?

options.text: It needs a larger window to hold three results at once during the final merge
options.says: Ruled out because "A larger context window does not fix attention quality."

options.text: It would hide real bugs found only occasionally, through the filter
options.says: Keeping only what two of three runs agree on would hide real bugs that are found only now and then (module 74, page 2). The remedy that fits the cause is to divide the work into a pass for each file and an integration pass. The page puts it as "would hide real bugs that are found only now and then".

options.text: It reports the same issues every time, so the filter changes nothing
options.says: Ruled out because runs differ, which is why the filter drops some bugs: "the same pattern may be flagged in one file and approved in another" and "real bugs that are found only now and then".

options.text: It repeats the integration pass, which already compares the results of runs
options.says: Ruled out because the integration pass is about files and not about runs: "A separate integration pass then looks at what crosses files".

origin.section: One pass over many files does not hold

questions.stem: Scenario S5. A script submits the overnight report to the batch interface, and an audit flags that its command lacks the headless flag. Is the finding right?

options.text: No, but only because batch jobs use a different flag for headless runs
options.says: Ruled out because "There is no headless environment variable and no `--batch` flag on the command line".

options.text: No, since that rule covers calls starting with the CLI, not a sender
options.says: A batch job's command is a script that submits the work, so the -p rule applies to commands that start with claude and not to a script (module 74, page 1). The page puts it as "a batch job's command is a script that submits the work".

options.text: Yes, since every command in a pipeline needs the flag to run unattended
options.says: Ruled out because the audit reports `no-print-flag` for "a command that starts `claude` without `-p` or `--print`", and a submitting script is no such command.

options.text: Yes, since batch jobs run through the interactive terminal tool
options.says: Ruled out because the batch is reached by "The Message Batches API, from a script".

questions.stem: Scenario S5. To keep a multi-file review consistent, each file's pass is shown the findings of the previous files. What does the page say about it?

options.text: It makes passes stop being independent, since earlier mistakes become premises
options.says: Seeing earlier findings makes the passes dependent, so earlier mistakes become premises, and consistency is the job of the cross pass (module 50, page 2). The page says "the passes become dependent and the earlier mistakes become premises".

options.text: It is wrong only for the last file, since its pass needs all of them
options.says: Ruled out because "Consistency is the job of the cross pass".

options.text: It is sound, since consistency needs shared memory
options.says: Ruled out because "Let the next file pass see the findings of the previous ones, for consistency" is rejected.

options.text: It is sound if the findings are summarised first, since summaries are neutral
options.says: Ruled out because a file pass "does not need to know how many other files there are or what they found", in any form.

questions.stem: Scenario S5. In a review with a pass for each file, one pass fails with an error, and the job script discards everything and starts over. What does the page advise?

options.text: Merge the failed file into the next pass
options.says: Ruled out because the passes stay independent, since otherwise "the passes become dependent".

options.text: Retry the failed pass until it succeeds, however long
options.says: Ruled out because "the subagent retries a bounded number of times", and not until it succeeds.

options.text: Report the breakage by name and let the other results stand
options.says: The failure is reported by file, and the rest goes on, since the other passes are valid (module 50, page 2). The page puts it as "The failure is reported by file, and the rest goes on".

options.text: Discard the whole review and start it again from the first file
options.says: Ruled out because "If one file pass fails, discard the review and start again" is rejected because "the other passes are valid".

questions.stem: Scenario S5. An audit of a pipeline flags its test-generation job for holding the edit tool, citing the rule that review jobs must only read. Is the finding right?

options.text: Yes, since writing test files is a way to change things in a production system
options.says: Ruled out because "The test-generation job is different on purpose: it writes test files, so it has `Edit`".

options.text: Yes, since every job in the pipeline must be read-only
options.says: Ruled out because the test-generation job "is not held to the read-only rule".

options.text: No, but only because a shell tool would be worse than the edit tool
options.says: Ruled out because the review "changes nothing, so its tools are `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob`".

options.text: No, since that limit binds inspections alone and this task writes by design
options.says: A review changes nothing, so its tools are Read, Grep and Glob, while test generation writes test files and is not held to the read-only rule (module 74, page 2). The audit checks the rule only for reviews. The page puts it as "The audit checks the rule only for reviews".

origin.section: The review reads, and nothing else
